Correction: Longtime enemy of competition. They know how much money online videos can make, and when only their video works well people will flock to it. It's obvious what they're trying to pull and yet they'll get away with it.

Actually, this is an attempt to eat away at the consumers' understanding of Net neutrality by presenting it in a positive, rather than negative manner; while pushing their own potentially lucrative streaming services. Unlike T-Mobile, they are being very selective in what services (their own) gets this benefit--but, honestly, both attempts are similar.

In a way, you can somewhat blame platforms like Netflix for relying on automatic streaming algorithms for some of this activity. They want to take as much advantage of whatever bandwidth is available to create the best quality for their platform, giving companies like T-Mobile an incentive to offer something like Bing-On--which is in itself a possible infringement of net neutrality--beneficial or otherwise.

If any of these companies really cared about the issue, they would put it in the hands of the consumer and stop attempting to mess with the prioritization of data. They would also allow the network itself handle the issue of quality--modern systems can do this pretty well

When you combine this with the ever-reducing cost of providing data to the consumer--last I checked it had fallen below $1 a GB for wireless and less than 1 cent for a wired connection--it isn't very hard to see that what they are trying to do is adjust the argument in a different direction and make violations of prioritization something with a positive overtone.
